title: Software Engineering in Practice
blurb: Requirements to production: design, reviews, quality gates, releases, observability, incidents, and team engineering.
description: A practical software-engineering course aligned to Aptech/ADSE-style analysis, design, Agile/DevOps and project delivery, without duplicating the dedicated Git, Testing, Architecture or CI/CD courses.

lessons.title: Engineering lifecycle: problem → production
objectives: Trace a feature from problem statement through production feedback.
Explain how software lifecycle changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect software lifecycle with delivery loop and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Professional software engineering is a feedback loop, not just coding. A feature begins with a problem and constraints, becomes an agreed requirement, gets designed and implemented in small reviewable changes, is verified, released, observed in production, and then improved using real feedback.
lessons.explain: Professional software engineering is a feedback loop, not just coding. A feature begins with a problem and constraints, becomes an agreed requirement, gets designed and implemented in small reviewable changes, is verified, released, observed in production, and then improved using real feedback.
commonMistakes: Starting implementation before the problem, constraints, and acceptance criteria are clear creates rework that good engineering process could have prevented.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Requirements, user stories & acceptance criteria
objectives: Turn a vague request into testable acceptance criteria.
Explain how requirements changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect requirements with user story and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A useful requirement describes observable behavior, not a preferred implementation. User stories can capture who needs what and why, but acceptance criteria make the request testable by defining examples, boundaries, and failure behavior.
lessons.explain: A useful requirement describes observable behavior, not a preferred implementation. User stories can capture who needs what and why, but acceptance criteria make the request testable by defining examples, boundaries, and failure behavior.
examples:
criteria = ["valid user can reset password", "expired token is rejected", "token can be used once"]
print("ready to implement:", all(bool(x.strip()) for x in criteria))
lessons.example:
criteria = ["valid user can reset password", "expired token is rejected", "token can be used once"]
print("ready to implement:", all(bool(x.strip()) for x in criteria))
commonMistakes: Writing “build password reset” as the whole requirement leaves security, expiry, error behavior, and completion criteria undefined.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Functional vs non-functional requirements
objectives: Separate what a system does from the qualities it must maintain.
Explain how functional requirements changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect functional requirements with latency and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Functional requirements describe behavior such as creating an order or searching a catalog. Non-functional requirements describe qualities and constraints such as latency, availability, privacy, capacity, auditability, and accessibility.
lessons.explain: Functional requirements describe behavior such as creating an order or searching a catalog. Non-functional requirements describe qualities and constraints such as latency, availability, privacy, capacity, auditability, and accessibility.
examples:
requirements = {"function":"search products","p95_ms":250,"availability":0.999,"max_results":50}
print(requirements)
lessons.example:
requirements = {"function":"search products","p95_ms":250,"availability":0.999,"max_results":50}
print(requirements)
commonMistakes: Treating “fast” or “reliable” as vague wishes instead of measurable constraints makes design decisions impossible to evaluate.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Design docs, ADRs & practical UML
objectives: Write a concise design decision with context, alternatives, and consequences.
Choose the lightest diagram that answers the team’s actual design question.
Use class, sequence, component, activity, and state diagrams to communicate structure, interactions, workflows, and lifecycle behavior.
lessons.explanation: Start from the question the diagram needs to answer. Use a class diagram for structure, a sequence diagram for interactions over time, a component diagram for major system parts, an activity diagram for workflow, and a state diagram for an object's states and transitions. Keep only the detail needed to explain the design.
lessons.explain: Start from the question the diagram needs to answer. Use a class diagram for structure, a sequence diagram for interactions over time, a component diagram for major system parts, an activity diagram for workflow, and a state diagram for an object's states and transitions. Keep only the detail needed to explain the design.
commonMistakes: Treating UML as paperwork or trying to draw every possible detail makes diagrams noisy and stale.
lessons.careerRelevance: Engineers use lightweight design docs, ADRs, sequence/component/state diagrams, and similar architecture sketches during feature design, code review, incident analysis, onboarding, and cross-team communication. The valuable skill is choosing the right artifact for the question and keeping it tied to the real system.

lessons.title: Repository structure & module boundaries
objectives: Organize code so responsibilities and dependency directions are obvious.
Explain how repository structure changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect repository structure with module boundary and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A repository should make the system easier to navigate. Good boundaries group code by responsibility and keep unstable details behind stable interfaces.
lessons.explain: A repository should make the system easier to navigate. Good boundaries group code by responsibility and keep unstable details behind stable interfaces.
examples:
layers = {"domain":[], "service":[], "adapters":[], "tests":[]}
for name in layers: print(name)
lessons.example:
layers = {"domain":[], "service":[], "adapters":[], "tests":[]}
for name in layers: print(name)
commonMistakes: Creating many tiny folders without a meaningful dependency boundary adds ceremony without reducing coupling.

lessons.title: Dependencies, environments & reproducible setup
objectives: Make a project installable and reproducible on another machine.
Explain how dependency management changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect dependency management with lockfile and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Dependencies are part of the program. A professional project records supported runtime versions, direct dependencies, locked versions where appropriate, configuration expectations, and setup commands.
lessons.explain: Dependencies are part of the program. A professional project records supported runtime versions, direct dependencies, locked versions where appropriate, configuration expectations, and setup commands.
examples:
requirements = {"python":"3.12", "fastapi":"0.115", "pytest":"8.x"}
print("documented runtime:", requirements["python"])
lessons.example:
requirements = {"python":"3.12", "fastapi":"0.115", "pytest":"8.x"}
print("documented runtime:", requirements["python"])
commonMistakes: “It works on my machine” is often a dependency or configuration specification failure, not a mysterious platform problem.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Coding standards, formatting & static analysis
objectives: Use automated checks to enforce cheap, repeatable quality rules.
Explain how style guide changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect style guide with formatter and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Formatting, linting, type checking, and static analysis catch different classes of problems. Automating these checks removes low-value style debates from review and finds issues before runtime.
lessons.explain: Formatting, linting, type checking, and static analysis catch different classes of problems. Automating these checks removes low-value style debates from review and finds issues before runtime.
examples:
checks = ["format", "lint", "type-check", "unit-tests"]
print("pre-review checks:", " -> ".join(checks))
lessons.example:
checks = ["format", "lint", "type-check", "unit-tests"]
print("pre-review checks:", " -> ".join(checks))
commonMistakes: Adding a tool with hundreds of warnings and no agreed policy often trains the team to ignore the tool entirely.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Git workflow: branches, commits & change size
objectives: Structure changes so history and review remain understandable.
Explain how branching changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect branching with atomic commit and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Professional Git usage is about change management. A branch isolates work, an atomic commit captures one coherent change, and a small pull request reduces review risk.
lessons.explain: Professional Git usage is about change management. A branch isolates work, an atomic commit captures one coherent change, and a small pull request reduces review risk.
examples:
commits = ["add idempotency validation", "test duplicate retry", "document API behavior"]
for c in commits: print("commit:", c)
lessons.example:
commits = ["add idempotency validation", "test duplicate retry", "document API behavior"]
for c in commits: print("commit:", c)
commonMistakes: A giant commit that mixes a feature, formatting, dependency upgrades, and unrelated refactors is difficult to review and dangerous to revert.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Pull requests & effective code review
objectives: Review correctness, design, tests, risks, and maintainability rather than only syntax.
Explain how pull request changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect pull request with code review and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Code review is a technical risk-control and knowledge-sharing process. The author should make the change easy to understand with a focused description, testing evidence, and notes about risky decisions.
lessons.explain: Code review is a technical risk-control and knowledge-sharing process. The author should make the change easy to understand with a focused description, testing evidence, and notes about risky decisions.
examples:
review = {"correctness":True,"tests":True,"security":"checked","rollback":"documented"}
print("merge ready:", all(v is True or isinstance(v,str) for v in review.values()))
lessons.example:
review = {"correctness":True,"tests":True,"security":"checked","rollback":"documented"}
print("merge ready:", all(v is True or isinstance(v,str) for v in review.values()))
commonMistakes: Reviewing only naming and formatting can miss a logically wrong or operationally unsafe change that looks clean.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Refactoring & technical debt
objectives: Improve structure without silently changing required behavior.
Explain how refactoring changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect refactoring with technical debt and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Refactoring changes internal design while preserving externally required behavior. Safe refactoring starts with tests or another behavior oracle, makes small transformations, and checks after each step.
lessons.explain: Refactoring changes internal design while preserving externally required behavior. Safe refactoring starts with tests or another behavior oracle, makes small transformations, and checks after each step.
commonMistakes: Rewriting a module from scratch and calling it refactoring removes the small-step safety that makes refactoring low risk.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Interface contracts & backward compatibility
objectives: Change an interface without unexpectedly breaking its consumers.
Explain how API contract changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect API contract with schema and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An interface contract includes inputs, outputs, errors, side effects, ordering, and compatibility expectations. Once other code or users depend on that contract, changing it becomes a coordination problem.
lessons.explain: An interface contract includes inputs, outputs, errors, side effects, ordering, and compatibility expectations. Once other code or users depend on that contract, changing it becomes a coordination problem.
commonMistakes: Renaming or removing a response field because “the new name is better” can break every consumer that still expects the old contract.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Test strategy & quality gates
objectives: Choose tests based on risk and place them at the right layer.
Explain how test strategy changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect test strategy with quality gate and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A test strategy connects risks to evidence. Unit tests give fast feedback on isolated logic, integration tests verify boundaries such as databases and APIs, and end-to-end tests cover a few critical user journeys.
lessons.explain: A test strategy connects risks to evidence. Unit tests give fast feedback on isolated logic, integration tests verify boundaries such as databases and APIs, and end-to-end tests cover a few critical user journeys.
examples:
risk = {"payment":"end-to-end + integration", "discount_math":"unit", "schema":"contract"}
for area,test in risk.items(): print(area, "=>", test)
lessons.example:
risk = {"payment":"end-to-end + integration", "discount_math":"unit", "schema":"contract"}
for area,test in risk.items(): print(area, "=>", test)
commonMistakes: Chasing 100% coverage can produce many low-value tests while important integration or failure behavior remains unverified.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Debugging with evidence & observability
objectives: Debug from evidence using hypotheses instead of random changes.
Explain how debugging changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect debugging with logs and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Effective debugging is a scientific loop: reproduce, gather evidence, form a hypothesis, run the smallest experiment that can disprove it, and narrow the search. Logs explain discrete events, metrics show trends and rates, and traces connect work across boundaries.
lessons.explain: Effective debugging is a scientific loop: reproduce, gather evidence, form a hypothesis, run the smallest experiment that can disprove it, and narrow the search. Logs explain discrete events, metrics show trends and rates, and traces connect work across boundaries.
examples:
events = [{"request":"r1","step":"validate"},{"request":"r1","step":"db-timeout"}]
print([e["step"] for e in events if e["request"]=="r1"])
lessons.example:
events = [{"request":"r1","step":"validate"},{"request":"r1","step":"db-timeout"}]
print([e["step"] for e in events if e["request"]=="r1"])
commonMistakes: Changing several things at once may make the symptom disappear while teaching you nothing about the actual cause.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Performance profiling & load testing
objectives: Measure before optimizing and distinguish latency, throughput, and resource bottlenecks.
Explain how profiling changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect profiling with benchmark and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Performance work starts with a target and measurement. Profiling identifies where time or memory is actually spent; microbenchmarks compare small operations; load tests reveal behavior under concurrency and sustained traffic.
lessons.explain: Performance work starts with a target and measurement. Profiling identifies where time or memory is actually spent; microbenchmarks compare small operations; load tests reveal behavior under concurrency and sustained traffic.
examples:
latencies=[80,90,95,110,400]
latencies.sort()
print("max sample latency:",latencies[-1],"ms")
lessons.example:
latencies=[80,90,95,110,400]
latencies.sort()
print("max sample latency:",latencies[-1],"ms")
commonMistakes: Optimizing the prettiest-looking loop without a profile can leave the real bottleneck—often I/O, database work, or contention—untouched.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Security & privacy in everyday engineering
objectives: Include basic security and privacy checks in ordinary feature work.
Explain how input validation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect input validation with least privilege and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Security is a property of normal engineering decisions: validating untrusted input, authenticating identities, authorizing actions, limiting permissions, protecting secrets, and minimizing sensitive data. Engineers should ask what the trust boundary is, what an attacker or accidental misuse could do, and what evidence will be recorded.
lessons.explain: Security is a property of normal engineering decisions: validating untrusted input, authenticating identities, authorizing actions, limiting permissions, protecting secrets, and minimizing sensitive data. Engineers should ask what the trust boundary is, what an attacker or accidental misuse could do, and what evidence will be recorded.
commonMistakes: Checking that a user is logged in is not the same as checking that the user is authorized to perform a specific action.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Semantic versioning, changelogs & releases
objectives: Communicate the scope and compatibility of a release.
Explain how semantic versioning changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect semantic versioning with changelog and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Version numbers and release notes are coordination tools. Semantic versioning expresses whether a public interface change is compatible, while a changelog explains what actually matters to users and operators.
lessons.explain: Version numbers and release notes are coordination tools. Semantic versioning expresses whether a public interface change is compatible, while a changelog explains what actually matters to users and operators.
examples:
release={"version":"2.1.0","change":"add optional export endpoint","breaking":False}
print(release)
lessons.example:
release={"version":"2.1.0","change":"add optional export endpoint","breaking":False}
print(release)
commonMistakes: Incrementing versions mechanically without documenting behavior changes gives downstream users no useful migration signal.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Documentation, runbooks & onboarding
objectives: Write documentation that helps someone perform a real task without tribal knowledge.
Explain how README changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect README with runbook and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Useful documentation is task-oriented. A README should explain purpose, setup, common commands, architecture entry points, tests, and contribution workflow.
lessons.explain: Useful documentation is task-oriented. A README should explain purpose, setup, common commands, architecture entry points, tests, and contribution workflow.
examples:
readme_sections=["Purpose","Setup","Run","Test","Architecture","Troubleshooting"]
print("README checklist:", ", ".join(readme_sections))
lessons.example:
readme_sections=["Purpose","Setup","Run","Test","Architecture","Troubleshooting"]
print("README checklist:", ", ".join(readme_sections))
commonMistakes: A README that only says the project name and how to install dependencies does not help a new engineer understand or operate the system.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Agile slicing, estimation & team collaboration
objectives: Break large work into small deliverable slices and communicate uncertainty.
Explain how vertical slice changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect vertical slice with estimation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Agile engineering is about short feedback cycles, not performing ceremonies. A vertical slice delivers a thin piece of end-to-end value that can be reviewed or tested.
lessons.explain: Agile engineering is about short feedback cycles, not performing ceremonies. A vertical slice delivers a thin piece of end-to-end value that can be reviewed or tested.
examples:
epic=["read-only endpoint","validation","write path","audit log"]
for slice_ in epic: print("deliverable slice:",slice_)
lessons.example:
epic=["read-only endpoint","validation","write path","audit log"]
for slice_ in epic: print("deliverable slice:",slice_)
commonMistakes: Splitting work by technical layer—“do all database work, then all backend work, then all UI”—can delay usable feedback until the end.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Incidents, postmortems & continuous improvement
objectives: Respond to failures and turn them into specific system improvements.
Explain how incident response changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect incident response with postmortem and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Incident response prioritizes user impact: detect, contain, communicate, recover, and then learn. A good postmortem reconstructs the timeline, contributing factors, detection gaps, and why safeguards did not catch the issue.
lessons.explain: Incident response prioritizes user impact: detect, contain, communicate, recover, and then learn. A good postmortem reconstructs the timeline, contributing factors, detection gaps, and why safeguards did not catch the issue.
examples:
postmortem={"impact":"12 min outage","contributing":["missing timeout","no canary"],"actions":["add timeout","canary deploy"]}
print(postmortem["actions"])
lessons.example:
postmortem={"impact":"12 min outage","contributing":["missing timeout","no canary"],"actions":["add timeout","canary deploy"]}
print(postmortem["actions"])
commonMistakes: Writing “engineer deployed bad code” as the root cause ignores the process and system controls that allowed one mistake to become an outage.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: End-to-end delivery capstone workflow
objectives: Combine requirements, design, implementation, review, release, and operations into one coherent workflow.
Explain how delivery changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect delivery with traceability and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Near-mastery means integrating the practices rather than memorizing them separately. For a real change, you should be able to show the requirement, acceptance criteria, design decision, implementation, automated evidence, review reasoning, release plan, production signals, and follow-up.
lessons.explain: Near-mastery means integrating the practices rather than memorizing them separately. For a real change, you should be able to show the requirement, acceptance criteria, design decision, implementation, automated evidence, review reasoning, release plan, production signals, and follow-up.
examples:

print(" -> ".join(artifacts))
lessons.example:

print(" -> ".join(artifacts))
commonMistakes: Treating process artifacts as unrelated paperwork creates duplication; each artifact should answer a different engineering question and connect to the next stage.
